question: Can a large, structured repository of executable agent skills be automatically created, quality-controlled, connected, retrieved, and composed so that agents solve tasks more successfully and efficiently across simulated environments and realistic workflows?

key_findings.claim: SkillNet represents skills as self-contained folders and organizes them through a three-layer ontology and a graph of prerequisites and compositions.
key_findings.evidence: The pipeline extracts skills from trajectories, repositories, documentation, and prompts; normalizes instructions and artifacts; filters and deduplicates candidates; and attaches taxonomy and dependency metadata. It reports more than 600,000 candidates and roughly 500,000 curated skills.

key_findings.claim: A GPT-5o-mini evaluator reportedly agrees closely with three doctoral-level human annotators on five skill-quality dimensions.
key_findings.evidence: Safety, completeness, executability, maintainability, and cost are combined with sandboxed code checks; on 200 skills the paper reports mean absolute error below 0.03 and quadratic weighted kappa above 0.90.

key_findings.claim: Benchmark-specific skills improve reward and reduce interaction steps in three embodied or web environments.
key_findings.evidence: Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld and four backbone models, skills synthesized from ETO expert trajectories yield the headline average relative gain of about 40% in reward and 30% reduction in steps versus no-skill agents.

key_findings.claim: The benchmark-specific gains do not establish transfer from the heterogeneous public repository.
key_findings.evidence: The evaluated environment skills are synthesized from ETO expert trajectories within the same benchmark families and are asserted not to overlap seen or unseen test tasks. They are not sampled from the broad GitHub, documentation, and prompt corpus advertised by the repository.

key_findings.claim: SkillNet-Gym evaluates retrieval and composition on 159 automatically constructed workflow tasks, but its ground truth is substantially co-generated by language models.
key_findings.evidence: LLMs infer preconditions, postconditions, and graph edges; Claude Code explores artifacts, writes golden solutions, and helps synthesize tests; candidate rollouts are used to strengthen weak tests; and three annotators inspect the retained tasks.

key_findings.claim: Model-based construction, post-hoc difficulty splits, and model-specific execution harnesses weaken evaluator independence.
key_findings.evidence: Tasks solvable by GLM-5.1 in all three no-skill attempts are removed; easy and hard categories are assigned from model outcomes; GPT-family evaluations use Codex while other models use Claude Code; and the same synthesized graph supplies retrieval and orchestration targets.

key_findings.claim: Skills help unevenly by domain and can actively hurt open-ended work.
key_findings.evidence: Domain analysis reports +50.0 points for geospatial tasks and +33.3 for data extraction, but -6.2 for academic research and -4.2 for business compliance; the authors attribute negative results to rigid guidance constraining exploration.

key_findings.claim: A larger retrieved skill set can degrade performance even when the needed skill is present.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix reports that a wild pool of more than 2,000 skills performs worse than the official subset, especially on hard tasks; Fabric retrieval has 100% candidate availability in the full pool but only 38.22% final full coverage under one configuration.

key_findings.claim: The reported failure modes include strong knowledge bias and instruction override, including stale APIs, workspace leakage, and template carryover.
key_findings.evidence: After initial manual inspection followed by AI-assisted classification, 59.6% of failures are assigned to knowledge bias and 40.4% to instruction override. The paper does not report the analyzed sample size or agreement for this failure taxonomy.

key_findings.claim: The breadth and security claims exceed the directly audited evidence.
key_findings.evidence: Only 200 skills receive the reported human comparison, whereas roughly 500,000 are curated; the limitations acknowledge incomplete coverage, unassessed skills, self-constructed quality, partially detected poisoned or adversarial content, and no end-to-end natural-language-to-agent system.

method.core_idea: Treat reusable agent know-how as executable, auditable folders connected by an ontology and dependency graph, then jointly evaluate skill quality, skill-conditioned task performance, retrieval, and multi-skill orchestration.
method.mechanism: LLMs extract and normalize instructions, code, resources, and metadata from several source types; heuristic, embedding, sandbox, and LLM checks filter and deduplicate them; a graph links prerequisites and compositions. SkillNet-Gym turns skill artifacts and graph paths into executable tasks with golden solutions and tests. SkillNet Fabric combines lexical, dense, graph, and encyclopedia retrieval before selecting and composing skills for an agent.
assumptions: A folder abstraction preserves enough procedural context to transfer across agents and tasks.
LLM quality scores and sandbox checks correlate with safe real-world usefulness at repository scale.
Automatically inferred graph edges represent true compatibility and ordering constraints.
Generated golden solutions and tests are sufficiently independent to validate generated tasks.
Benchmark-specific expert-derived skills are informative about the broader public skill ecosystem.
Differences between Codex and Claude Code harnesses do not dominate model comparisons.

techniques.role: Packages instructions, code, resources, examples, and metadata into a portable unit.
Generates candidates from expert trajectories, repositories, documentation, and prompts.
Places skills in a three-layer taxonomy for browsing, retrieval, and coverage analysis.
Represents prerequisite, composition, and related-skill structure.
Combines executable checks with LLM ratings of safety and usability.
Fuses BM25, dense, graph, and external-knowledge signals in SkillNet Fabric.
Creates pre/postcondition tasks, golden solutions, and deterministic tests from skill artifacts.

evaluations.setting: Two hundred skills rated by GPT-5o-mini and three doctoral-level annotators.
evaluations.metric: Mean absolute error and quadratic weighted kappa over five quality dimensions.
evaluations.result: Reported MAE below 0.03 and QWK above 0.90.
evaluations.baseline: Aggregated human ratings on the selected 200-skill audit sample.

evaluations.setting: ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with four backbone models and benchmark-specific skills synthesized from ETO expert trajectories.
evaluations.result: Headline average relative reward improvement of roughly 40% and step reduction of roughly 30% versus no skills.
evaluations.baseline: No-skill agents and comparisons with ReAct and Expel-style prompting.

evaluations.setting: SkillNet-Gym's 159 retained executable tasks across multiple domains and difficulty levels.
evaluations.metric: All-tests-pass binary score and Avg@k over three runs.
evaluations.result: Skills benefit harder tasks more than easy tasks, while one-shot composition remains weak and some domains regress.
evaluations.baseline: No-skill execution and alternative skill-context configurations.

evaluations.setting: SkillRouterHard with 75 routing queries over 79,141 candidate skills.
evaluations.metric: Recall and full-coverage rate at K=5 and K=10.
evaluations.result: SkillNet Fabric reports 67.91 recall and 49.33 full coverage at K=5, increasing to 74.80 and 60.0 at K=10.
evaluations.baseline: Lexical, dense, graph-only, and other routing baselines under the same pool.

evaluations.metric: Task success or pairwise LLM-judged quality, depending on benchmark.
evaluations.result: Fabric improves retrieval and composition metrics, but the AgentSkillOS portion relies on model-based pairwise judgment.
evaluations.baseline: Alternative retrieval and orchestration systems evaluated in the respective benchmark harnesses.

limitations: Author-stated: repository coverage remains incomplete and the quality of automatically constructed skills is not guaranteed.
Author-stated: a substantial portion of the skill collection has not received direct assessment.
Author-stated: poisoned, malicious, and adversarial skills are only partly detected.
Author-stated: the work does not provide a complete natural-language-to-agent construction system.
Reviewer inference: no matched token, context, tool-call, or execution budget cleanly isolates skill content from extra inference compute.
Reviewer inference: result tables lack sufficient seed-level uncertainty for strong claims about heterogeneous tasks and backbones.

Reviewer inference: the 200-skill evaluator audit does not demonstrate reliability over a half-million-item, long-tailed repository, and sampling composition and evaluator-development independence are unclear.
Reviewer inference: model-generated tasks, graph edges, golden solutions, and tests create circularity that deterministic pass/fail execution alone cannot remove.
Reviewer inference: the benchmark-specific ETO skills demonstrate within-family reuse, not open-world cross-domain transfer.
failure_modes: A retrieved skill can encode an obsolete tool version, wrong parameter, or hidden workspace assumption.
A rigid skill template can override task-specific instructions and reduce performance on exploratory research or compliance tasks.
Additional relevant and irrelevant skills can flood context and lower full-task coverage despite perfect candidate availability.
A poisoned skill can pass shallow quality filters and become amplified by graph retrieval.
Model-generated tests can validate the same assumptions embedded in a model-generated golden solution.
A task-filtering model can remove its own easy cases and make later model comparisons creator-dependent.
Different execution harnesses can be mistaken for differences in backbone ability or skill use.
Embedding and MD5-based deduplication can miss semantically duplicated, lightly rewritten, or contaminated instructions.
reusable_insights: Evaluate skill usefulness conditionally on query, model, harness, tool version, and token budget rather than assigning one global score.
Keep skill source, dependency, version, permission, and execution-test provenance visible to both agents and humans.
Use independent task authors, hidden tests, and cross-backbone execution to break generator-evaluator circularity.
Include a no-skill abstention option and penalize harmful retrieval; more context is not monotonically better.
Measure transfer on new task families and environments, not only held-out instances derived from expert traces in the same benchmark.
Red-team stale APIs, prompt override, workspace leakage, and poisoned dependencies as first-class skill failure classes.
open_questions: What fraction of the public repository remains beneficial under pinned tools, hidden tests, and independent human review?
Can a router predict when using no skill is safer than retrieving a superficially relevant one?
How stable are skill rankings across model families, execution harnesses, context budgets, and tool versions?
Can skill graphs be learned from causal execution evidence rather than inferred textual compatibility?
How should skills be revoked or repaired when upstream tools or dependencies change?
Does automatically generated procedural knowledge improve open-ended research once compute and context are matched?

competitive_landscape.title: SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct benchmark competitor and contrary evidence
competitive_landscape.difference: SkillsBench uses 86 tasks across 11 domains with deterministic grading and finds curated skills help by 16.2 points but self-generated skills have no average gain and 16 of 84 skill-task pairs regress; this directly narrows SkillNet's broad creation claims.

competitive_landscape.title: SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering?
competitive_landscape.difference: SWE-Skills-Bench evaluates 565 software tasks and reports only 1.2% average gain, with 39 of 49 skills yielding zero improvement and version mismatch causing losses up to 10%; SkillNet reports larger gains in more synthetic or benchmark-specific settings.

competitive_landscape.title: How Well Do Agentic Skills Work in the Wild: Benchmarking LLM Skill Usage in Realistic Settings
competitive_landscape.difference: This benchmark scales retrieval to roughly 34,000 skills and finds benefits collapse toward no-skill performance under realistic routing, while query-specific refinement helps; it challenges SkillNet's repository-scale extrapolation.

competitive_landscape.title: SkillLearnBench: Benchmarking Continual Learning Methods for Agent Skill Generation on Real-World Tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: SkillLearnBench compares continual skill-generation methods on real tasks and finds external feedback helpful but self-feedback vulnerable to recursive drift, whereas SkillNet focuses repository construction and does not isolate continual self-improvement dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: Organizing, Orchestrating, and Benchmarking Agent Skills at Ecosystem Scale
competitive_landscape.difference: AgentSkillOS uses hierarchical retrieval and dependency-aware composition over pools up to 200,000 skills and introduces a 30-task benchmark; SkillNet scales the repository further and adds Fabric but relies partly on AgentSkillOS's model-judged evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: SkillGenBench: Benchmarking Skill Generation Pipelines for LLM Agents
competitive_landscape.difference: SkillGenBench pins environments, fixes execution harnesses, uses deterministic checks, and separates task-conditioned from task-agnostic generation across repository and documentation sources; it isolates generation effects more cleanly than SkillNet's end-to-end stack.

competitive_landscape.title: OpenSkillEval: Automatically Auditing the Open Skill Ecosystem for LLM Agents
competitive_landscape.difference: OpenSkillEval dynamically audits open skills on 600 tasks and reports that popularity is not predictive and skill effects interact with model and framework; SkillNet assigns scalable intrinsic quality scores but validates few skills directly.

competitive_landscape.title: Skill Is Not Document: A Query-Conditional Benchmark and Two-Stage Retriever for LLM Agent Skill Routing
competitive_landscape.difference: This work formalizes skill routing as joint query-skill compatibility and introduces a query-conditional benchmark showing document relevance is insufficient; SkillNet Fabric combines more signals but uses graph-derived targets that are less independent.

competitive_landscape.title: SkillWeaver: Web Agents can Self-Improve by Discovering and Honing Skills
competitive_landscape.difference: SkillWeaver discovers, practices, and refines skills within web environments for self-improvement; SkillNet targets a much larger cross-source ecosystem and graph, but its strongest task gains still use environment-specific expert traces.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: SkillNet is a web-scale infrastructure for creating, evaluating, connecting, retrieving, and composing agent skills, with a half-million-item curated repository and large gains in agent task performance.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper combines a folder standard, three-layer ontology, dependency graph, scalable quality evaluator, 159-task generated gym, and hybrid Fabric router; benchmark-specific skills improve reward and efficiency in three environments.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The integration and scale are distinctive, but evidence for universal skill transfer is not. SkillsBench, SWE-Skills-Bench, wild-retrieval studies, and SkillLearnBench report null or negative effects under broader or more realistic conditions. SkillNet's own -6.2 academic-research result, large-pool degradation, model-generated benchmark, harness confound, and limited human audit make the defensible claim a promising infrastructure prototype rather than a validated universal skill layer.

reviewer_notes: All 34 extracted pages were read, including the task-generation, filtering, wild-pool, and annotation appendices. The audit distinguishes the more than 600,000 candidates from approximately 500,000 curated skills and does not treat benchmark-specific ETO-derived skills as evidence that arbitrary internet skills transfer. Competitor titles, URLs, and result-level deltas were checked against primary arXiv records on 2026-08-23. Evaluator agreement is reported as an author claim because sampling composition, class balance, and independence from evaluator development are not documented sufficiently for an external reliability conclusion.
